claims_disputed.claim: Token consumption falls 21.6% and total cost 33.6%.
claims_disputed.reason: Beyond the AgentDiet framing the review flags, the cost advantage over no compression is not robust: for Qwen3-Coder-30B AttnCompress is slightly more expensive than Original in Table 1 ($0.0551 vs $0.0546) and in the 5-run Table 2 ($0.0566 vs $0.0563). The -20.2% vs Original is carried by the Gemini/Qwen-235B single runs. Compression cost is priced at Qwen API rates although the method needs proxy attention weights (run on 8x A100).

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The paper reports costs and tokens thoroughly but does not evaluate a budget or cap mechanism; cost reporting is not evidence that token budgets/caps work.

missed_issues: Internal inconsistency on latency: §5.1 says proxy compression takes 66.6 s of 366.7 s end-to-end, but Table 6 lists Ana Time 530.87 s for the default Qwen3-4B proxy with Qwen3-Coder-30B, and the text's claim that 4B has 'substantially lower analysis time than the 8B proxy' (384.1 s) contradicts Table 6.

In Table 2 (the only repeated-run evidence) AttnCompress is below uncompressed Original on pass rate (43.70 vs 44.10) and equal on cost, i.e. for that model there is no measured trade-off benefit at all.
Proxy-model variation (Table 6: 43.5-46.5% on Qwen3-Coder) is as large as the method-vs-baseline gaps, so the 'default' choice of Qwen3-4B is not clearly better than alternatives, and 8B beats it.
Relevance should be lower (2): the mechanism requires attention access to an open-weight proxy inside the agent loop, which the review itself notes commercial mixed hosts do not expose.
note: First review is careful and correctly downgrades the headline; I add that the cost saving vs full context disappears for Qwen3-Coder and that the latency numbers are internally inconsistent.
